Putting greens for a town built around two golf communities

Backyard putting greens in Clermont run $14–$30 per square foot as of September 2026. Between Kings Ridge and Legends Golf & Country Club sitting across the street from each other, a lot of Clermont homeowners already play regularly, which makes a contoured green a natural extension of a game they're already in rather than a new hobby.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Contouring a green on a lot that already slopes

Everywhere else we work, contouring a putting surface means building undulation into an otherwise flat base on purpose. In Clermont, the lot itself often supplies part of that contour before the design even starts, which can work in a green's favor or against it depending on which direction the grade runs. A green laid across the slope, rather than straight down it, usually plays truer and drains more predictably than one that fights the existing grade.

The fringe and cup placement still follow the same build regardless of the starting grade: a firm, level pad under each cup, and fringe turf transitioning cleanly to whatever surrounds it, whether that's a natural lawn or a bed.

Nylon or textured polyethylene for the putting surface?

A Clermont putting green's playing surface is built from either short nylon or textured polyethylene fiber, cut far shorter than any lawn turf so a ball rolls across the tips of the blades rather than settling into them. Nylon holds its shape and stiffness longer under repeated ball contact and foot traffic, while textured polyethylene offers a softer feel underfoot at a lower cost. Neither fiber choice changes the base or drainage requirements underneath; the decision comes down to how firm the roll should feel and how much daily play the surface is expected to take.

Say you have a 400 sq ft green built into a gentle backyard slope

A 400 sq ft green with a two-cup layout, built into a lot that falls about a foot across its width, runs $14–$30 a square foot, or $5,600 to $12,000 depending on how much contouring and fringe the design carries. Using the existing grade for part of the break, rather than flattening it first, typically keeps the shaping cost from climbing toward the top of that range the way building break from scratch on a flat lot can.

Fringe turf usually adds a modest amount beyond the green's own square footage once it wraps the perimeter, which is worth accounting for when comparing a quote against the raw putting-surface number alone.

A green for a golf-community backyard versus a hilltop lot

In Kings Ridge or Legends, a small green tends to fit into an already-landscaped rear yard behind a lanai, sized to match a footprint that's been fixed since the home was built. Further up toward the ridge's newer streets, a hilltop lot can carry a larger green with more break built in, since the yard itself hasn't been shaped around existing hardscape the way an older gated-community lot has.

Either way, an ARC submittal in a community with design review wants the same basics: dimensions, a sample of the turf, and where the green sits relative to the lot line, the same packet the state HOA statute assumes exists before covering what an association can and can't restrict.

Low-E glass near a pool-cage green

Greens built inside or beside a screened pool cage are common in Clermont, and a west-facing sliding door or low-emissivity window nearby is worth checking before finalizing the layout, since reflected sunlight from that kind of glass can soften turf enough to damage it. The fringe around a green, made from polyethylene that starts to give around 175 to 200°F, is more exposed to this risk than the nylon putting surface itself, which tolerates heat somewhat better. A scorched patch along one edge of an otherwise undamaged green usually traces back to exactly this kind of reflection.

Keeping a green's base off the septic drainfield

A Clermont yard with a septic system needs its drainfield and pump-out lid located before staking a putting green's tiers, since the deeper four- to six-inch excavation a green requires disturbs more ground than a flat lawn conversion does, and the state's rule still requires that lid stay reachable once the green is finished. A green's shaped contours make working around a fixed access point harder than it would be on open lawn, so the design usually routes tiers and cup locations away from that spot entirely rather than trying to shape a break around it. This gets settled before any digging starts.

What the ridge's sand means for a green's subbase

Candler sand, common across the ridge, drains so fast on its own that the usual concern with a putting green base elsewhere, water sitting under the surface and softening the roll, mostly doesn't apply here. The base still needs the same washed, open-graded crushed rock the state's rule requires, compacted firm enough that a rolled putt doesn't develop a soft spot near the cup after a season of play.

What the sand does add is the same erosion consideration as a residential lawn: a green built into a slope needs its edges anchored well enough that heavy rain doesn't undercut the fringe at the low end over time. What a Florida putting green costs breaks the price range down further by feature.

Infill and a roll test before calling the job done

The last step on a Clermont green is a thin, even layer of infill followed by a roll test, checking that a ball tracks true across the surface rather than pulling toward one side from uneven grooming or nap direction. Adjustments at this stage are usually small, a pass with the brush in a different direction, or a bit more infill in one section, rather than anything structural, since the base and surface work is already finished by this point. Skipping the roll test and assuming a green plays correctly because it looks finished is how a pulling break goes unnoticed until the first real game.

Grooming more often in the dry months, differently in the wet ones

A Clermont green needs more frequent light grooming through the dry season, since dust and pollen build up without rain to clear them and a consistent roll depends on keeping the surface free of both. Once June through September rainy season sets in, storms handle some of that clearing on their own, but grooming right after a storm rather than days later matters more here than in the dry months, since damp infill settles differently under a brush than dry infill does. Matching the routine's frequency and timing to the season keeps stimp speed more consistent across the whole year instead of drifting between wet and dry stretches.

Questions people ask

Can a Clermont lot's natural slope replace built-in contouring?

Partly. A gentle existing grade can supply some of a green's break, which can lower the shaping cost, but cup placement and a level pad under each cup still need to be built regardless of the starting slope.

Do Kings Ridge or Legends require a specific putting-green design?

Neither has a published design document we could find naming synthetic greens specifically. An ARC submittal with dimensions, a product sample and a site plan is the standard packet either community's review committee is likely to expect.

Is Clermont the only nearby town with golf-community putting greens?

No. Four Corners and the resort corridor toward Minneola both carry golf-adjacent subdivisions where a home green is a common request, though Clermont's Kings Ridge and Legends pairing is the densest concentration in our south Lake County coverage.
